title: Chapter 14 — The Trade Of Literature
paragraphs: Democracy not only spreads a taste for letters among the trading classes but also introduces a trading spirit into literature. In aristocracies, readers are fastidious and few in number. In democracies, they are far more numerous and far less difficult to please. The consequence is that among aristocratic nations no one can hope to succeed without immense exertion, and that this exertion may bring a great deal of fame but can never earn much money. Among democratic nations, on the other hand, a writer may flatter himself that he will cheaply obtain a modest reputation and a large fortune. For this purpose he need not be admired; it is enough that he is liked. The ever-growing crowd of readers, and their constant craving for something new, assure the sale of books that nobody much esteems.

In democratic periods the public often treats authors as kings treat their courtiers: they enrich them and they despise them. What more do the venal souls born in courts, or worthy of living there, need? Democratic literature is always infested with a tribe of writers who regard letters as a mere trade, and for the few great authors who adorn it, you may count thousands of idea-peddlers.
